question.prompt:
Mr. Ramos gave a test to his class of \(20\) students. The dot plot below shows the distribution of test scores.

[Figure 1](figures/2022_AMC_8_Q19_question_fig1.svg)

Later Mr. Ramos discovered that there was a scoring error on one of the questions. He regraded the tests, awarding some of the students \(5\) extra points, which increased the median test score to \(85.\) What is the minimum number of students who received extra points?

(Note that the median test score equals the average of the \(2\) scores in the middle if the \(20\) test scores are arranged in increasing order.)

solutions.explanation:
For \(20\) scores, the median is the average of the 10th and 11th scores in increasing order. The dot plot initially puts both of those scores at \(80\).

The plot has \(13\) scores at \(80\) or below. Each can increase by at most \(5\), so at least \(13\) scores remain at \(85\) or below. Thus neither middle score can end above \(85\). To have their average equal \(85\), both must therefore become \(85\). In particular, the 10th score must be \(85\), meaning at least \(11\) scores must be \(85\) or higher.

The original plot has only \(7\) scores at least \(85\), so at least \(11-7=4\) students need extra points.

This minimum is possible: increase four of the five scores of \(80\) to \(85\). Then exactly \(9\) scores remain below \(85\), and the 10th and 11th scores are both \(85\).

The answer is \(\boxed{4}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\). A minimum argument needs both a lower bound and a way to attain it.
solutions.title: Count scores that must cross the new median threshold
